topic.title: Only three units left
topic.claim: 'Only three units left at this price' at a site visit is a price ladder, not a shortage.
topic.moment: The sales lady says the price goes up next week, and the cheque book suddenly feels urgent.

turn.actually: Builders release stock in slabs and raise the price each slab, so 'last units' is always true.

topic.feeling: Rushed into the biggest cheque of my life.
topic.villain: Phased inventory releases built into builder pricing
topic.because: Each price step rewards early buyers on paper and pushes late ones to hurry. The builder controls how many units are 'left'.
topic.payoff: Ask how many units are unreleased, not how many are left.
topic.behaviour: Builders announce price hikes by phase and run 'limited' offers at site visits.
topic.send_to: The couple doing site visits every Sunday
topic.why_now: Festive launches just pushed a wave of 'new phase' pricing.

score.why: 'Last units' is always true because the builder controls what's released. The sharp question to ask is how many units are unreleased.

notes: slide 5: 'The next fifty are waiting behind it, at a new price.' The 'fifty' is an invented count that reads like data. Either drop the number ('The whole next phase is waiting behind it, at a new price.') or replace it with the sourced example: Ashiana Housing's director said prices on its Gurugram project Amarah 'more than doubled between Phase 1 and Phase 4'. Keep that wording exactly. Do not make it stronger.

slide 7: 'Scarcity here isn't measured. It's scheduled.' This repeats the 'isn't X. It's Y.' structure from slide 1 ('isn't a shortage. It's a price ladder'), so the post starts to feel engineered. Recast it as a plain statement, for example: 'The builder controls the count. The shortage is on a calendar.' That keeps the sting without echoing the cover.

slide 7: The UP RERA line is the post's best receipt, but it sits after the mechanism line and lands like a news add-on. Lead into it with why it matters: a regulator had to publicly warn people about this exact sales line. For example: 'It's common enough that UP RERA warned buyers about "limited stock" and "price hike" messages. Over 1.15 lakh units were unsold across the state.' That makes the fact back the opinion instead of standing alone.

slide 4: This is the most explainer-like slide ('They release it in slabs: phase one, phase two, phase three.'). Add one detail only an insider would notice, still framed as typical. For example, the rate card on the sales table quietly changes its date while the brochure stays the same. That keeps the slide in the reader's room, not in a textbook.

slide 9: 'That fear is exactly what the slab is priced to use.' This states a deliberate design as fact. Soften the mechanism, not the voice: 'That fear is what the slab runs on.' It stays sharp without claiming a plan you can't show.

mechanism.broken_premise: None. The premises hold as descriptions of common practice, with two caveats. (1) No law says each phase must cost more. Phase-wise escalation is a builder's choice, and a builder can hold or cut prices, or offer discounts, when stock isn't selling. UP RERA's own advisory says the market is 'not running out of inventory'. (2) The 1.15 lakh figure counts all available stock, including flats, villas, plots, shops and offices. It is not only unsold flats, and it dates from a June 2026 advisory. Neither caveat breaks the argument.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: The RERA Act lets a promoter register and develop a project in phases, and each phase counts as a separate project with its own registration, unit count and timeline. That is why a builder can open inventory in tranches and reprice each one. 'Only three left' can be literally true for the current tranche or price band while the builder decides when the next units go on sale. The builder can't hide totals, though: each registered phase's unit count and progress are filed on the state RERA portal. So the post's tip to ask how many units haven't been released can be checked there instead of relying on the salesperson.

sources.quote: The availability of 1.15 lakh properties in Uttar Pradesh reflects the wide variety of housing.
Planning to buy a home? UPRERA says don't fall for 'limited stock' claims
Such claims are often used to create pressure on buyers to make immediate bookings.

Where the real estate project is to be developed in phases, every such phase shall be considered a stand alone real estate project, and the promoter shall obtain registration under this Act for each phase separately.

sources.fact: UP RERA warned buyers that promoters and agents use limited-stock and imminent-price-hike claims to create urgency, while data shows over 1.15 lakh unsold units statewide.
sources.excerpt: UPRERA warned against "misleading messages claiming limited stock or imminent price hikes." ... promoters and agents "create a sense of urgency by claiming that property prices are set to rise sharply" ... "current market data does not indicate any shortage of inventory," and more than 115,000 units are available statewide.

sources.fact: Ashiana Housing's Gurugram project Amarah raised prices phase by phase, with remaining Phase 4 units priced at least 10% above Phase 3.
sources.excerpt: Varun Gupta, Director of Ashiana Housing, says "the prices have more than doubled between Phase 1 and Phase 4." He adds that "the remaining units in Phase 4 may be priced at least 10% higher than Phase 3 prices." The remaining 112 Phase 4 units are expected to sell at a 10% higher price.

_ledger.text:
[cover] 'Only three units left' is a [price ladder], not a shortage.
The builder decides how many flats are left.
 

[slide 1] 'Only three units left at this price' isn't a shortage. It's a price ladder.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] Every Sunday site visit ends the same way. Sample flat, cold coffee, a floor plan on the table.
Then the soft line: 'Sir, is price pe sirf teen units bache hain. Next week se rate badh raha hai.'

[slide 3] And it works. A couple who came 'just to see' starts asking about the token amount.
The biggest cheque of your life gets written on a weekend, in an AC room, against a countdown.

[slide 4] Builders don't put the whole project on sale at once. They release it in slabs: phase one, phase two, phase three.
Each slab comes with a higher rate per square foot.

[slide 5] So 'only three left' is true. Three are left in this slab. The next fifty are waiting behind it, at a new price.

[slide 6] On a 1,000 sq ft flat, a ₹500 jump per square foot is ₹5 lakh.
Same flat. One week later.

[slide 7] The builder controls the count. The shortage runs on a calendar.
UP RERA itself warned buyers about 'limited stock' and 'price hike' messages, while over 1.15 lakh units sat unsold across the state.

[slide 8] The ladder has a sweetener built in. When the rate card changes, early buyers see their flat 'go up' on paper.
They tell every relative the project is hot. The hike on phase two sells phase three.

[slide 9] Nobody's dumb for rushing. A flat costs a decade of salary now.
Missing the 'old rate' feels like losing money you never had. The slab is priced for exactly that feeling.

[slide 10] Next site visit, skip 'how many are left?'
Ask how many haven't been released yet. Then watch how long the answer takes.

[end card] Read it again before you hand over the token cheque at your next site visit.
Send to the couple spending every Sunday in sample flats, sure the good rate is about to disappear.

It mentions UP RERA warning buyers about limited-stock and price-hike claims while over 1.15 lakh units were unsold in the state. It ends by telling the reader to ask how many units are unreleased, not how many are left.

'Only three units left at this price' isn't a shortage. It's a price ladder.
Swipe to read →
Every Sunday site visit ends the same way. Sample flat, cold coffee, a floor plan on the table. Then the soft line: 'Sir, is price pe sirf teen units bache hain. Next week se rate badh raha hai.'
And it works. A couple who came 'just to see' starts asking about the token amount. The biggest cheque of your life gets written on a weekend, in an AC room, against a countdown.
Builders don't put the whole project on sale at once. They release it in slabs: phase one, phase two, phase three. Each slab comes with a higher rate per square foot.
So 'only three left' is true. Three are left in this slab. The next fifty are waiting behind it, at a new price.
On a 1,000 sq ft flat, a ₹500 jump per square foot is ₹5 lakh. Same flat. One week later.
The builder controls the count. The shortage runs on a calendar. UP RERA itself warned buyers about 'limited stock' and 'price hike' messages, while over 1.15 lakh units sat unsold across the state.
The ladder has a sweetener built in. When the rate card changes, early buyers see their flat 'go up' on paper. They tell every relative the project is hot. The hike on phase two sells phase three.
Nobody's dumb for rushing. A flat costs a decade of salary now. Missing the 'old rate' feels like losing money you never had. The slab is priced for exactly that feeling.
Next site visit, skip 'how many are left?' Ask how many haven't been released yet. Then watch how long the answer takes.
